text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Volvo posted a profit for the first half of the year above market expectations and its seems healthy profits could continue. Like telecoms group Ericsson, the company will consider outsourcing some of its activities.
- Some 51 percent of participants in a skills-building course sponsored by the National Labour Board found jobs.

- Sweden's financial watchdog is critical of the newly-merged Foreningssparbankens' proposal to work with independent savings banks. The finance inspectorate says the banks must indicate to customers if they are part of the new group or just working with it.
- Swedish exports to southeast Asia have developed strongly in the past few years but a currency crisis in the region could cause exports to level off.

- A 37-year-old Russian is awaiting deportation to Moscow, accused of being part of a swindle involving diverting state aid to a hospital in Murmansk into private pockets. The Russian led a life of luxury in Sweden and the joint Russian/Swedish police operation has revealed the extent of money laundering operations between the two countries.
- Sweden now has the highest interest rates among the so-called "garlic belt" after Italian rates fell below Swedish on Monday.
- Sales and profit development for vehicle maker AB Volvo are good but profitability is still unsatisfactory.
- The average working week in Sweden is 38.5 hours long and the 40-hour-work week exists only in theory, statistics from Swedish employers group SAF show.
- Published only on Fridays in the summer.
